title: ClawHub TradingView assistant skills deliver the "cluw" macOS infostealer via a rentry.co paste-site lure
summary: On 2026-05-17 one ClawHub account published two macOS "TradingView AI assistant" skills — `tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant` and `ai-tradingview-assistant-for-macos`. Both refuse to work until the agent follows a mandatory prerequisite block pointing at hxxps://rentry[.]co/openclaw-code, which serves a base64 string to paste into a terminal. Running it fetches hxxp://2.26.75[.]16/Xuvewuyur, a macOS infostealer that Unit 42 tracks as `cluw`. The delivery template is the ClawHavoc one, but the backend is fresh: neither the C2 host nor the payload family matches the earlier AMOS infrastructure. ClawHub's automated audit returned Pass for one skill and no verdict for the other until mid-May 2026.
details:
**Chain (Unit 42):** SKILL.md prerequisite block → paste-site redirect lure at `rentry[.]co/openclaw-code` → base64 command → `2.26.75[.]16/Xuvewuyur` → `cluw` infostealer (SHA-256 `818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7`). Unit 42 notes the structure is verbatim the pattern that characterised over 300 skills in the original ClawHavoc disclosure (SKA-2026-0001), which is exactly why a paste-site indirection defeats IOC-only blocking: the published skill never changes when the operator swaps the payload behind the paste link.

**Skill digests published by Unit 42:** `b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007` (tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant) and `881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7` (second skill hash listed in the same IOC table; Unit 42 does not map each hash to a file name explicitly).

**What a deterministic scanner sees:** an imperative "you must run this before the skill works" prerequisite (`prompt-injection`), a base64-decode-into-shell step (`dangerous-commands`), and a raw-IP fetch-and-execute (`dangerous-scripts`). What it does *not* see is the paste-site content itself — SkillWarden never fetches remote URLs, so the malicious half of this chain lives outside the scanned artifact (docs/THREAT-MODEL.md, R1/R2).

**Fact vs. inference:** skill names, publication date, lure URL, C2 host, payload name and hashes are as published by Unit 42 (2026-06-23), which redacts the publisher account. Unit 42 reported all five skills in its article to ClawHub; OpenClaw banned the accounts and removed the skills. Attribution to the ClawHavoc operators is explicitly *not* asserted by Unit 42 — it notes the template is shared while the infrastructure is new. Verified 2026-08-04.
